title: GOD TOLD A NEW HUSBAND TO STAY HOME FOR ONE YEAR—AND THE REASON SHOULD SHAKE EVERY MARRIAGE TODAY
paragraphs: GOD TOLD A NEW HUSBAND TO STAY HOME FOR ONE YEAR—AND THE REASON SHOULD SHAKE EVERY MARRIAGE TODAY

Before God sent a newly married man into battle, He commanded him to do something many husbands have forgotten: stay with his wife, protect their first year together, and bring happiness into her life. Buried in Deuteronomy 24:5 is a breathtaking revelation about love, marriage, responsibility, and the heart of a God who never intended a covenant to become a lonely prison.
Imagine being a newly married woman in ancient Israel.

The wedding celebration is over. The guests have returned home. The songs have faded into memory. Your new husband is beside you, and for the first time, the two of you are beginning a life that neither of you has ever lived before.
There are dreams to build. Fears to confess. Habits to understand. Disagreements to navigate. A home to establish.
You barely know what tomorrow will look like.
Then suddenly, someone comes to your door.
Your husband is needed.
There is a battle to fight. A national responsibility to fulfill. Something important enough to pull him away from the woman he has just promised to love.
You stand there, wondering whether the man you married will return.
And then something extraordinary happens.
God's Law speaks.
Not to demand that the newlywed husband immediately leave his bride.
Not to dismiss her loneliness as insignificant.
Not to treat their marriage as an inconvenience standing in the way of greater responsibilities.
Instead, Scripture declares:

"When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither shall he be charged with any business: but he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken." — Deuteronomy 24:5, KJV
Read that final phrase again.
"And shall cheer up his wife."
Not merely provide a roof.
Not merely put food on the table.
Not merely give her his surname and expect gratitude.
He was to devote that first year to his new marriage, including bringing happiness to the woman he had taken as his wife.
And the deeper you examine the original Hebrew, the more remarkable this command becomes.
Because God was not simply protecting a honeymoon.
He was protecting the beginning of a covenant.
The Hebrew text contains these words:
נָקִי יִהְיֶה לְבֵיתוֹ שָׁנָה אֶחָת וְשִׂמַּח אֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ אֲשֶׁר־לָקָח
Nāqî yihyeh ləvêtô shānāh ʾeḥāt, vəśimmaḥ ʾet-ʾishtô ʾasher-lāqaḥ.
A close rendering is:
"He shall be free for his household for one year, and he shall make glad his wife whom he has taken."
Pay attention to the Hebrew word וְשִׂמַּח (vəśimmaḥ).
It comes from the root שָׂמַח (śāmaḥ), associated with rejoicing, gladness, and joy.
Here, the verb is in a form that conveys causing someone to rejoice or making someone glad.
This is why translations express the phrase as "cheer up his wife," "bring happiness to his wife," or "make his wife happy."
The original language does not merely describe a husband's private happiness.
It directs his attention toward his wife's well-being.
There is something deeply moving about that.
In a world where armies needed soldiers, fields needed workers, and households carried serious responsibilities, the Law of Moses recognized that a new marriage also needed time.
And that time was not treated as worthless.
It was protected.
The command even excluded the newly married man from military service and certain public obligations during that first year.
Deuteronomy 20:7 had already instructed that a man who was betrothed but had not yet completed his marriage should return home rather than go into battle, lest he die before marrying.
Deuteronomy 24:5 goes further by protecting the first year after marriage.
The context matters.

This was a civil and covenantal law given to ancient Israel, not a universal command requiring every Christian husband today to quit his employment or remain physically inside his house for twelve months.
Nor does it mean that a husband can guarantee his wife's happiness, as though another person's every emotion were under his control.
But the principle is unmistakable.
Marriage was never meant to receive only whatever attention remained after everything else had taken its share.
And perhaps that is where this ancient command begins speaking painfully to modern hearts.
Because somewhere tonight, a woman is lying beside a man she loves, wondering when he stopped noticing her.
He is physically present.
His phone is glowing.
His mind is somewhere else.
She has spent the day caring for children, carrying responsibilities, managing exhaustion, and silently swallowing frustrations she no longer knows how to explain.
She wants to talk.
He wants to sleep.
She wants to feel understood.
He thinks paying the bills should already prove everything.
And neither knows how to say what is really happening.
They are not necessarily enemies.
They may still love each other.
But somewhere between earning a living and maintaining a household, they have begun forgetting how to nurture the relationship that brought them together.
And this is where we must be careful.
It would be unfair to turn Deuteronomy 24:5 into a weapon against hardworking husbands.
Many men are exhausted because they are trying desperately to provide.
Some leave home before sunrise and return after dark because their families need food, medicine, rent, and school fees.
Some carry pressures their wives never fully see.
And some wives are equally exhausted, carrying responsibilities their husbands have never fully understood.
The Bible is not inviting us to despise provision or ignore sacrifice.
It is inviting us to recognize that providing for a marriage and nurturing a marriage are related responsibilities, but they are not identical.
A paycheck can help sustain a household.
It cannot, by itself, replace tenderness.
A beautiful house can shelter a family.
It cannot, by itself, create emotional safety.
And a wedding ceremony can establish a marriage.
It cannot, by itself, sustain intimacy through the years that follow.
Love must be lived.
Not just announced.
Not just remembered on anniversaries.
Lived.
In ordinary conversations.
In forgiveness after arguments.
In the willingness to listen when listening is inconvenient.
In the humility to admit, "I have been here physically, but I have not really been present with you."
And perhaps the most painful words in some marriages are not "I don't love you anymore."
Perhaps they are the words nobody says:
"I miss the person you used to be with me."
There is a remarkable connection between this ancient command and another passage in Scripture.
Genesis 2:24 says:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh."
The Hebrew verb translated "cleave" comes from דָּבַק (dāvaq), meaning to cling, hold fast, or remain closely attached.
This is covenant language.
Marriage requires a new primary human loyalty.
A husband does not simply add a wife to a crowded list of competing priorities.
He enters a relationship that changes how he orders his life.
And the wife, too, enters a covenant of shared faithfulness, responsibility, and love.
This does not mean spouses abandon their parents, neglect their children, or refuse every other obligation.
It means their marriage deserves intentional care rather than perpetual leftovers.
Think about how easily the opposite happens.
Before marriage, two people may stay awake for hours just to hear each other's voices.
After marriage, they can sit together for hours without truly speaking.
Before marriage, they notice the smallest sadness in each other's faces.
After marriage, they sometimes overlook pain that has been building for months.
Before marriage, they find ways to spend time together.
After marriage, they sometimes assume the relationship will survive without the attention that once helped it grow.
And slowly, without a dramatic betrayal or a single unforgettable argument, distance begins to settle into places where affection once lived.
Not every marriage experiences this.
But enough do that we should pay attention.
Because neglect does not always announce itself loudly.
Sometimes it arrives disguised as busyness.
Sometimes it sounds like, "We'll talk tomorrow."
And tomorrow becomes next week.
Next week becomes next month.
Until two people who promised to share their lives begin living separate emotional lives under the same roof.
But Deuteronomy 24:5 is not merely a warning about neglect.
It is a reminder that the God of Scripture cared about the beginning of a marriage long before modern relationship counselors began discussing intentional connection.
And the New Testament develops the responsibility of marital love even further.
Ephesians 5:25 declares:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it."
Now the standard becomes even more demanding.
The husband is not simply told to create pleasant experiences.
He is commanded to love sacrificially.
And the model is Jesus Christ.
Not domination.
Not entitlement.
Not emotional manipulation.
Not demanding respect while refusing to show tenderness.
Christ loved the church by giving Himself.
His love was not self-serving.
It was costly.
It was faithful.
It moved toward the people He came to redeem.
And when Paul commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, he gives marriage a pattern of self-giving love that challenges selfishness at its roots.
But this also means we must reject a dangerous distortion.
Christlike sacrifice never gives anyone permission to abuse, intimidate, control, or harm a spouse.
The call to forgiveness is not a command to remain in immediate danger.
The call to reconciliation does not eliminate the need for repentance, accountability, protection, and genuine change.
Jesus did not teach us to disguise cruelty as holiness.
His love exposes darkness rather than asking people to pretend it is light.
And if we want to understand marriage through the Gospel, we must never separate love from truth.
Consider another passage.
Colossians 3:19 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them."
That final command matters.
Because sometimes a marriage is not destroyed by the absence of grand romantic gestures.
Sometimes it is wounded by the repeated presence of harshness.
A cutting remark.
A dismissive answer.
An eye roll.
A cruel joke.
A refusal to apologize.
A habit of treating strangers with more patience than the person waiting at home.
And Scripture speaks directly into that.
A husband cannot faithfully claim to follow the self-giving love of Christ while deliberately cultivating bitterness toward his wife.
Neither can a wife dismiss her own calling to love, honor, and faithfulness.
Marriage is not a competition to determine which spouse deserves more compassion.
It is a covenant in which both are called to walk in humility before God.
Philippians 2:3–4 instructs believers to reject selfish ambition and consider the interests of others.
That instruction is not limited to marriage, but it certainly belongs inside it.
Imagine what would change if both spouses began asking a different question.
Not merely, "Why aren't you making me happy?"
But, "How can I love you more faithfully today?"
Not, "Why don't you understand me?"
But, "Have I really tried to understand what you are carrying?"
Not, "Who started this argument?"
But, "What would humility, truth, and repentance look like right now?"
This does not erase real wrongdoing.
It does not make every conflict simple.
And it does not place the responsibility for repairing a marriage equally on a faithful spouse and an abusive one.
But where two people are willing to turn toward God and toward one another, these questions can begin changing the atmosphere of a home.
And there is another truth we must not overlook.
Deuteronomy 24:5 does not promise that the newly married couple would never experience hardship.
It does not say that one protected year would guarantee a lifetime without grief.
It does not claim that marriage would eliminate loneliness, disappointment, sickness, financial pressure, or human weakness.
It simply recognizes that the beginning of a marriage deserves intentional protection.
The command is beautiful precisely because it takes human vulnerability seriously.
New love can be joyful.
And new love can be fragile.
Two imperfect people are learning to share a life.
They need patience.
They need understanding.
They need time.
And sometimes, the most spiritual thing a husband can do is not deliver another speech about leadership.
It is to sit beside his wife and genuinely listen.
Sometimes, the most loving thing a wife can do is not pretend everything is fine.
It is to speak truthfully, with grace, about what has been hurting.
Sometimes, the next faithful step is a sincere apology.
Sometimes it is seeking wise pastoral counsel or qualified marriage counseling.
Sometimes it is putting the phone down.
Sometimes it is praying together after months of spiritual silence.
And sometimes it is simply saying:
"I know we have both been tired. But I don't want us to become strangers. Can we begin again?"
That question may be small.
But it can open a door.
Still, we must go deeper.
Because even the most devoted husband cannot become his wife's savior.
And even the most loving wife cannot become her husband's redeemer.
This is where a beautiful teaching about marriage must lead us beyond marriage itself.
Our deepest need is not simply a better spouse. Our deepest need is Jesus Christ.
A marriage can be strengthened by better communication, healthier boundaries, wise counsel, and renewed commitment.
Those things matter.
But no human relationship can carry the weight of being someone's ultimate source of identity, salvation, or eternal hope.
Only Christ can reconcile sinners to God.
Only Christ can forgive sin through His saving work.
Only Christ can give the new life that human effort cannot manufacture.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
There is the heart of the Gospel.
We were not rescued because we had finally become worthy of love.
Christ died for sinners.
He did not wait for us to repair every failure before revealing the depth of His mercy.
He came into a broken world.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
That is why the message of grace is so much greater than relationship advice.
Marriage may reveal our selfishness.
Conflict may expose our pride.
Disappointment may uncover wounds we thought we had buried.
But Jesus meets us at the deeper problem: the sin that separates us from God.
And He calls us to repentance, faith, and newness of life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
This does not mean every broken marriage will automatically be restored.
It does not mean trust can be rebuilt without accountability.
It does not mean a repentant person can demand immediate forgiveness or reconciliation on their own terms.
But it does mean that our past failures do not have to be the final word over our relationship with God.
In Christ, sinners can be forgiven.
Proud hearts can learn humility.
Harsh people can learn gentleness.
Self-centered people can learn sacrificial love.
And wounded people can discover that their dignity and worth do not depend on another person's ability to love them well.
Perhaps you are reading this as a husband.
And something in you has become quiet.
You remember when your wife smiled more easily around you.
You remember when she reached for your hand without hesitation.
You remember conversations that did not end in defensiveness.
And perhaps you are beginning to recognize how often you have given your best attention to everyone except her.
If that is you, do not turn conviction into another excuse for despair.
Bring it to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Apologize without adding excuses.
Ask what she has been experiencing.
And let your actions begin demonstrating the love your words have promised.
Not for one dramatic evening.
Not merely until the argument disappears.
But through faithful, ordinary consistency.
Perhaps you are reading this as a wife.
And tears are gathering because you cannot remember the last time you felt genuinely cherished.
You have tried explaining.
You have tried staying quiet.
You have tried becoming easier to love.
And somewhere along the way, you began wondering whether your longing for kindness was unreasonable.
It is not unreasonable to desire respect, affection, honesty, and faithful care in marriage.
You are not required to pretend that emotional neglect or mistreatment is good.
You may need a truthful conversation, trustworthy support, or wise counsel.
And if you are facing abuse, your safety matters. Seek appropriate help and protection.
The Lord sees what other people overlook.
Psalm 34:18 says:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."
That promise does not guarantee that every earthly relationship will become what we hoped.
It does remind us that brokenhearted people are not invisible to God.
Perhaps you are unmarried.
Or widowed.
Or divorced.
Or still carrying the memory of a relationship that ended painfully.
Do not hear this passage as though God's affection is reserved for married people.
It is not.
The same Scriptures that honor marriage also honor faithful singleness.
Paul speaks positively of singleness in 1 Corinthians 7.
Jesus Himself lived without marrying.
Your worth is not measured by whether someone has chosen you as a spouse.
Your deepest identity is found in your relationship with God.
And perhaps you are someone who has failed in marriage.
Not accidentally.
Not merely because life became difficult.
You know you sinned.
You betrayed trust.
You spoke cruelly.
You neglected someone who loved you.
You made promises you did not keep.
And now the consequences are real.
Please understand this.
Grace is not permission to minimize what happened.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the damage never existed.
But the Gospel announces that sinners may come to Christ in genuine repentance and find mercy.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
The way forward begins with truth.
Not performance.
Not religious appearances.
Not blaming the person you hurt.
Truth.
Confession.
Repentance.
And the willingness to bear the responsibilities that genuine change requires.
That is what makes the Gospel so astonishing.
Jesus does not merely offer us a better public image.
He offers forgiveness and transformation.
And sometimes the most powerful evidence of grace is not a dramatic testimony spoken before thousands.
Sometimes it is a man who finally stops defending his harshness.
A woman who finds the courage to speak truth.
A couple who seeks help before resentment becomes permanent.
A parent who apologizes to the family.
A believer who stops using Bible verses to justify selfishness.
A heart that stops hiding and begins surrendering.
That is where the theme of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus erases every consequence.
Not because every human story ends with the reunion we wanted.
But because the cross and resurrection proclaim that sin, shame, and failure need not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
And now return to that newly married couple in ancient Israel.
Imagine the husband hearing the command.
He is free from military service for a year.
He is given time to establish his home.
He is told to bring gladness to his wife.
Perhaps he expected marriage to be something he could fit around all his other duties.
Instead, the Law required him to recognize the significance of the covenant he had entered.
And perhaps that is the question this passage leaves before us today.
What are we protecting with our time—and what are we allowing to quietly disappear?
We protect appointments.
We protect income.
We protect schedules.
We protect reputations.
We protect our phones with passwords and our possessions with locks.
But are we protecting the relationships God has entrusted to us?
Are we protecting time for prayer?
Are we protecting our hearts from bitterness?
Are we protecting the truth of the Gospel from being reduced to religious appearances?
A marriage does not become holy merely because two people call themselves Christians.
It is shaped by the daily practice of faithfulness, truth, humility, forgiveness, and love.
And the first year of marriage is not the only year that matters.
The tenderness that deserves protection at the beginning remains worthy of care in the fifth year.
The twentieth.
The fortieth.
Even when the faces have aged.
Even when the hands are no longer young.
Even when life looks nothing like the wedding photographs.
The covenant still calls for faithfulness.
And if your marriage has become painfully distant, you do not need to pretend otherwise.
You can begin with one truthful conversation.
One prayer.
One apology.
One decision to seek help.
One act of love that asks for nothing in return.
Not because a single gesture can repair years of damage.
But because faithfulness is lived one real decision at a time.
If this message has uncovered something you have been avoiding, do not rush past that conviction.
Bring it before Jesus.
Your story may encourage someone who believes change is impossible.
And if you are still struggling, you do not need to reveal private details publicly to prove your faith.
The Lord hears prayers whispered where nobody else can see.
Maybe a husband who has confused provision with presence.
Maybe a wife who has been quietly wondering whether her pain matters.
Maybe an engaged couple who needs to understand that a wedding is the beginning of a covenant, not the completion of one.
Maybe a believer who needs to remember that the Gospel calls us to repentance as well as comfort.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter Scripture, examine their hearts, discover the grace of Jesus Christ, and grow through faithful discipleship.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue reaching people with the Gospel, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing another inspirational article.
The desire behind this ministry is to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through biblical teaching, Christian encouragement, discipleship, and resources that help believers grow in faith.
We want to continue making biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who cannot afford to pay for it.
That mission takes time, work, resources, and faithful support.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
But they are one way we can thank those who choose to stand alongside the work.
Pray for the ministry.
Help a struggling believer discover biblical encouragement.
Point someone who has lost hope back toward Christ.
No one should feel pressured to give what they cannot afford.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
We simply invite those who are willing and able to partner with us as we continue proclaiming the One who gave Himself for sinners.
Because at the end of everything, our purpose is not to build a following around a personality.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
The Savior who forgives.
The Savior who transforms.
The Savior who teaches us how to love.
The Savior whose grace reaches even into the places where we have failed.
And now, one final thought.
Deuteronomy 24:5 tells us that a newly married husband in Israel was given a year free from certain national obligations so he could devote himself to his home and bring gladness to his wife.
It is a beautiful command.
But the greater beauty of Scripture is that every good and holy gift ultimately directs our attention toward the goodness of God.
A faithful marriage can reflect Christlike love.
It cannot replace Christ.
A devoted husband can bring gladness to his wife.
He cannot give her eternal life.
A loving wife can strengthen and encourage her husband.
She cannot remove his sins.
Only Jesus can do what no husband, wife, wedding vow, or human promise could ever accomplish: reconcile us to God through His death and resurrection.
So love your spouse while you have the opportunity.
Speak the words that should not remain unspoken.
Repent of the sins you have been excusing.
Seek help where healing requires it.
Cherish the people entrusted to your care.
And above everything else, cling to Jesus Christ.
Because one day, the schedules will no longer matter.
The unfinished work will pass into history.
The possessions we struggled to acquire will belong to someone else.
And the moments we thought we could always recover will be gone.
Do not become so busy building a life together that the person beside you spends that life quietly waiting to be loved.
